faq.q: Why is rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia dangerous?

faq.a: Standard ORS is low in potassium; add banana or coconut water for modest K replacement.
faq.q: Can oral rehydration solution correct potassium loss?

faq.a: Treat as high‑risk: give calcium gluconate IV to stabilise the heart while arranging labs.
faq.q: What is the first step if a patient has severe hyperkalaemia but no ECG?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with severe diarrhoea presents with muscle cramps and K 2.8 mmol/L — what is the immediate management and why avoid rapid IV potassium? — Give oral/IV potassium chloride in divided doses, monitor ECG; rapid large bolus can cause hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia.

A patient on chronic thiazide therapy develops confusion, serum Na 122 mmol/L, and no edema — differentiate acute vs chronic hyponatraemia and outline safe correction limits. — Chronic: >48 h, correct ≤8 mmol/L/24 h; acute: may need faster but still ≤12 mmol/L/24 h.
You receive a lab report of K 6.2 mmol/L but the sample is haemolysed — how do you proceed? — Repeat the sample; if repeat unavailable, treat as hyperkalaemia because haemolysis overestimates K.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with polyuria, bone pain, and serum Ca 1.8 mmol/L — what are the likely causes and next steps? — Renal calcium loss and vitamin D deficiency; give calcium supplementation and vitamin D, assess renal function.

A malaria patient receives quinine and develops sudden drop in Na to 128 mmol/L — what is the mechanism and how to manage? — Quinine causes SIADH; restrict free water, consider hypertonic saline if symptomatic.

A postpartum woman on magnesium sulfate for eclampsia develops absent reflexes and K 6.0 mmol/L — explain the link and immediate action. — Magnesium shifts K out of cells; stop magnesium, give calcium gluconate, treat hyperkalaemia.

A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with hyperphosphataemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism — how does this affect calcium and what preventive measures help? — Phosphate retention lowers Ca, stimulates PTH; use low‑phosphate diet, calcium carbonate binders, vitamin D analogues.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Electrolyte disorders are common, often multifactorial, and can be life‑threatening. Recognise patterns, use limited investigations wisely, and treat the underlying cause while correcting the imbalance.

b: Hyponatraemia < 135 mmol/L, Hypernatraemia > 145 mmol/L
Hypokalaemia < 3.5 mmol/L, Hyperkalaemia > 5.5 mmol/L
Hypocalcaemia < 2.1 mmol/L, Hypercalcaemia > 2.6 mmol/L
sections.p: A disturbance in serum concentrations of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate or bicarbonate that produces clinical signs or requires treatment.

b: Mild: asymptomatic, electrolyte 5‑10 % outside normal range
Moderate: symptoms (muscle cramps, nausea) or 10‑20 % deviation
Severe: life‑threatening signs (arrhythmia, seizures, coma) or >20 % deviation
sections.p: Severity guides urgency of correction and monitoring intensity.

b: Sodium loss: diarrhoea, cholera, vomiting, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency
Sodium excess: hypertonic saline, salt‑rich herbal teas, diabetes insipidus with excess water intake
Potassium loss: diarrhoea, vomiting, loop/thiazide diuretics, renal tubular acidosis, sickle‑cell crises with renal loss
Potassium excess: AKI, tumour lysis, potassium‑rich IV fluids, herbal potassium supplements
Calcium loss: malnutrition, vitamin D deficiency, chronic diarrhoea, phosphate binders
Calcium excess: hyperparathyroidism, excessive calcium carbonate, milk‑alkali syndrome
Magnesium loss: prolonged diarrhoea, malnutrition, aminoglycosides, antimalarials
Magnesium excess: renal failure, excessive antacid use
sections.p: Identify the dominant physiologic disturbance (loss, excess intake, redistribution, renal handling).

b: Hyponatraemia: headache, nausea, seizures, coma; rapid fall > 10 mmol/L in 24 h is dangerous
Hypernatraemia: thirst, confusion, focal neurologic deficits, seizures
Hypokalaemia: muscle weakness, cramps, constipation, ECG U‑waves, ventricular arrhythmias
Hyperkalaemia: paresthesiae, muscle weakness, peaked T‑waves, ventricular fibrillation
Hypocalcaemia: tetany, Chvostek sign, prolonged QT
Hypercalcaemia: polyuria, stones, abdominal pain, lethargy, shortened QT
sections.p: Symptoms reflect the specific ion and the speed of change.

t.a: Serum electrolytes (Na, K, Ca, Mg, PO4, HCO3)
t.b: What is the exact ion disturbance and its magnitude? Guides urgency of treatment
Does the electrolyte abnormality affect cardiac conduction? Detects hyper‑kalaemia, hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia changes
Is the kidney conserving or wasting the ion? Distinguishes renal vs extrarenal loss
Are there contributing metabolic or renal causes? Important for potassium and bicarbonate management

b: Severe hyponatraemia with seizures or coma
Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes
Hypocalcaemia with tetany or cardiac arrest
Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia → osmotic demyelination
Over‑rapid potassium repletion → hyperkalaemia
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents irreversible organ damage.

b: Stop offending drugs (e.g., diuretics, potassium supplements)
Replace losses with appropriate IV fluids: 0.9 % saline for Na loss, 5 % dextrose with K‑free saline for K loss, calcium gluconate IV for severe hypocalcaemia
Use oral repletion when possible: rice‑water solution for Na, banana/ORS for K, dairy or calcium carbonate for Ca
Avoid rapid shifts: limit Na correction to ≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h, K repletion not > 0.5 mmol/L per hour, Ca correction not > 0.2 mmol/L per hour
Consider binding resins (e.g., calcium polystyrene sulfonate) for chronic hyperkalaemia if dialysis unavailable
sections.p: Treat the cause first, then correct the ion safely.

b: Repeat serum electrolytes 4‑6 h after acute correction, then daily until stable
Counsell on avoiding excessive herbal remedies containing potassium or sodium
Provide ORS packets for diarrhoea, encourage balanced diet rich in fruits/vegetables
Screen for chronic kidney disease in patients with recurrent abnormalities
sections.p: Re‑check electrolytes after any intervention and educate on safe fluid/medicine use.

b: Hyponatraemia vs pseudohyponatraemia (hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidaemia) – check serum osmolality
Hyperkalaemia vs ECG artefact – verify with repeat sample
Metabolic acidosis vs respiratory alkalosis – use arterial blood gas
sections.p: Distinguish true electrolyte disturbance from mimics.

b: Haemolysis raises serum potassium falsely
Delayed processing lowers calcium due to binding to proteins
Low‑quality dipsticks may underestimate urine sodium
sections.p: Laboratory artefacts are common in low‑resource labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain, severe arrhythmia, or cardiac arrest from hyperkalaemia
Tetany, laryngeal spasm, or sudden loss of consciousness from hypocalcaemia
